title: Results Supplementary Info
text:
I aggregated buffer data by their spatial clustering because otherwise there would be pseudoreplications due to closely spaced points. This meant averaging calculated continuity statistics for Guezen and Forrest’s data by the “site” identity since their points were transects that were closely spaced (within ~ 1km) inside site groups. Aaron’s data had “farm” groupings but these didn’t always mean they were closely spaced. Instead, I grouped points that were 1km within each other and averaged them. Hemberger and Williams’s sites were selected to be more than 1km apart so I didn’t have to do this for their data. Instead of averaging, I could also have randomly selected one point in each group and used that to calculate continuity statistics, but I think the results will be similar.
The aggregation process resulted in 149 total points (27 Guezen & Forrest, 35 Hemberger & Williams, and 87 Iverson). The % natural area vs crop shannon diversity is shown below.









I’m focusing on three statistics summarizing temporal change in floral resources:

The mean floral resources across time points
The coefficient of variation across time points - I’ve switched back to CV because the behavior of “stability” (1/CV) seems funny to me. As differences between time points approach perfect equality, CV gets smaller, so the stability value approaches infinity. This results in a heavy emphasis on sites where floral resources almost didn’t change at all, which creates outliers.
The scaled peak time represents the weighted mean flowering time on a unit scale that represents the entire “season” of each study. To calculate, I took the average of the time points weighted by their flower counts and then scaled by the number of timepoints used in the study, so max flowering time across all studies was one. This is a method that performed well in a comparison of peak flowring estimates by Taylor (2019).
For Aaron’s data, I used the 5-timepoint subset.

For each of the stats I fit generalized linear models with % natural area and crop shannon diversity as predictors. I used likelihood ratio tests to compare models with linear relationships to quadratic ones, and with interactions.

title: Results Supplementary Info
section: Mean floral resources over the season
text:
Mean floral resources over the season

Plots





Percent natural area against mean floral resources over time. Floral resource means have been z-scaled based on their associated study’s distribution. Points are colored by location shannon diversity and shape is study.









Crop shannon diversity against mean floral resources over time. Floral resource means have been z-scaled based on their associated study’s distribution. Points are colored by location % natural area and shape is study.






Model comparisons
I use normal distribution linear regression to fit standardized floral counts. I used a Gamma distribution GLM before for fitting the unstandardized counts, but once standardized, the final linear regression doesn’t show any issues. I also fit a dispersion parameter that varies by study, since the plots suggest that each study’s values are differently dispersed.
Base model:
glm.flrmn1 <- glmmTMB(flr.mn.zscale ~ crop.shandiv + pct.natural + study, 
                      dispformula = ~ study,
                      data = all.mn)
Likelihood ratio tests comparing linear model to quadratic % natural area or quadratic crop shannon diversity. Quadratic natural area term is supported, while quadratic crop shannon diversity is not.


Data: all.mn
Models:
glm.flrmn1: flr.mn.zscale ~ crop.shandiv + pct.natural + study, zi=~0, disp=~study
glm.flrmn2a: flr.mn.zscale ~ crop.shandiv + poly(pct.natural, 2) + study, zi=~0, disp=~study

title: Project flowers
text:
Iverson data
Aaron took surveys of all vegetation within a larger area using a modified Whitaker plot. Herbaceous plants were measured by coverage and trees were counted. Flowers were not counted during the survey but instead counted at peak flowering density independently of the site. The average peak flower density (or per-individual count for trees) was used to define the flowering curve that was calculated for the site over the entire year. Aaron’s workflow calculates total flower area per ha using floral dimensions from literature or field measurements, but I stop at flower counts to match the other studies.

title: Continuity
text:
Date ranges of datasets differ. Hemberger & Williams (2025) collected data at 5 timepoints from 2003-02-20 to 2003-07-30. Guezen and Forrest (2021) collected data from 4 timepoints from 2016-05-20 to 2016-09-01.
Since Iverson has estimates for every day, I limit continuity calculation from 2016-03-01 to 2016-09-30, which is when there are significant flowers predicted. As an alternative, to see if it matters, I also tried sampling midway through each month in the full range (7 months), and for a truncated range of 2016-04-15 to 2016-08-15 (5 months) that matches the other studies’ dates better.





Flowering curves from Iverson data. Solid vertical lines show extent used for calculating coefficient of variation for entire season; black dotted lines show sampled time points across the full range; orange dashed lines show the truncated points of sampling.

title: Continuity
text:
Continuity distributions
For Aaron’s data, I wanted to compare differences in coefficient of variation between the full range of dates and the subsampled dates. There is significant correlation between the full range and sampled dates. If 7 sample dates are used, then the scatter of points in this comparison is around the 1:1 line (fig below). But if 5 sample dates are used to sample, the CV values estimated from 5 samples (orange points, below) are lower than the CV estimated from 7 samples.





The coefficient of variation for the full set of data (daily floral counts) is shown on the x-axis. The y axis is for the sampled CV values. Black points compare the full dataset CV to CV of sampled data across 7 months. Orange points compare the full dataset CV to sampled data across 5 months. Red line is the 1:1 line.





Comparison of distributions
Site continuity values by study. Hemberger & Williams (2025) has 5 timepoints, Guezen & Forrest (2021) has 4 timepoints, and three versions of CV calculated for Aaron’s data using 5 timepoints, 7 timepoints, and 214 timepoints (daily values).









Another way to measure continuity is stability, which is 1/cv. This feels a little more intuitive to me because higher values correspond to higher stability, which I’m interpreting as continuity.









It seems like the data would be more comparable if we limited Aaron’s data to 5 samples. The CV values and stability values are in a similar range to the other datasets.

The relationship between % natural and crop shannon diversity / crop richness
There’s an upper limit to crop diversity/richness in the plots below, which decreases as % natural reaches 100%. I believe this is determined in part by field size. You can only have one crop per field, and you can only have so many fields as crop area decreases. Exploratory models
I fit the following models and then compare their AIC. A three-way interaction is most supported, which suggests the slopes between % natural and crop richness interact, and the relationships change between studies.

Three-way interaction model predictions
Significant interactions between the variables seem to be mainly driven by a strong interaction between % natural and crop richness for the Guezen & Forrest (2021) study. Slopes mostly aren’t significantly different from zero across these variables’ interactions for the other two studies.
